transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (StratusTek Head of Security), Ethan Cole (CTO), Lina Park (DevOps), Tom Hsu (Legal)

(00:00) Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining we have about 45 minutes on the calendar, quick intros from our side daniel is our solutions engineer who will walk through the technical bits and i'll handle the procurement and security docs follow up
(00:12) Priya Singh: thanks maya yeah i'll be leading this from security; quick note we're evaluating hosted and private options, primary constraints are KMS integration and audit log retention; uh we also need to understand how RBAC maps to our existing org roles
(00:28) Ethan Cole: and from an infra POV we care about latency for inference, but security trumps millisecond wins if there's a compliance blocker
(00:40) Daniel Ortiz: totally makes sense; just to set expectations we support three deployment modes hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, and private/vpc on-prem. each has different controls around network, key management, and logging. we'll run through specifics and can point to the SOC2 and ISO artifacts as well
(01:05) Lina Park: when you say private do you mean full on-prem interconnect or VPC peering? curious about egress paths
(01:15) Daniel Ortiz: we do both — private deployment can be a customer-managed VPC with a control plane or a fully air-gapped on-prem package depending on needs. for VPC we do peering or private link equivalents, egress can be blocked and logs forwarded to your splunk/elk
(01:40) Priya Singh: ok good can you explain key rotation for KMS? we need to use our HSM, not Redwood-managed keys
(01:50) Daniel Ortiz: yes, BYOK supported. for hosted we support customer KMS via IAM cross-account grants and you can rotate keys on your schedule; for dedicated and private you have direct KMS integration and HSM-backed KMS is compatible — there are a couple of config steps. i'll add the detailed steps to the diagram
(02:10) Tom Hsu: any SOC 2 scope limitations? our legal team needs evidence of Type II for the last 12 months and any subservice orgs
(02:22) Maya Chen: we have SOC2 Type II, we can share the report under an NDA; also ISO 27001 summary available. i'll send the redacted report, it's standard for enterprise folks
(02:38) Priya Singh: good, also need to confirm audit log retention — we have to keep certain logs for 7 years for financial transactions. is that possible?
(02:50) Daniel Ortiz: by default Redwood retains platform audit logs for 90 days in the console but we have export hooks to push logs to customer S3, splunk, or their SIEM. for private deployments you can configure indefinite retention in your environment; hosted customers routinely export to long-term storage for retention compliance
(03:10) Ethan Cole: what's included in 'platform audit logs' — model prompts, PII, admin actions? need to know what is considered PII flow-through
(03:21) Daniel Ortiz: logs capture API call metadata (timestamps, model, route, token counts), deployment events, role changes, and high-level errors. We intentionally avoid logging full prompt content in plaintext for hosted by default; customers can opt-in to store transcripts if they want. for regulated PII we recommend the private option so data never leaves your network and you control storage encryption
(03:55) Priya Singh: that matches our thinking — private looks favorable. however we need to evaluate latency and cost; daniel can you run through batching and quantization options that affect latency/cost?
(04:10) Daniel Ortiz: yeah on the runtime side we do continuous batching; for low-latency paths we reduce batch sizes and pin to high-priority pools, which increases cost. quantization reduces memory and cost but can slightly affect quality depending on model; for private you can pick specific kernel optimizations and pinned hardware for consistent latency
(04:35) Lina Park: how does RBAC work for API tokens and UI access? we use SCIM for provisioning and want okta as our IdP
(04:45) Maya Chen: we have SSO with SAML2.0 and full SCIM provisioning; RBAC is role-based per-organization with predefined roles and fine-grained permissions for models, routes, and billing. you can create service accounts with scoped permissions and rotate API keys. we'll share the admin guide
(05:05) Priya Singh: does redwood support conditional access policies or device posture checks?
(05:12) Daniel Ortiz: we integrate with IdP controls for MFA and can propagate group claims to RBAC. conditional access is handled by your IdP; Redwood respects the auth token context but doesn't enforce device posture itself in hosted mode — in private you can front with your own access gateways for that
(05:35) Ethan Cole: on encryption at-rest, with BYOK what parts are encrypted with our keys — model weights, KV cache, logs?
(05:45) Daniel Ortiz: data at rest in private is under your control; with BYOK we encrypt model caches, persistent stores, and any KVS using your keys. In hosted, user data blobs and artifacts can be encrypted with customer keys for storage and backups; ephemeral runtime caches use ephemeral keys but can be wrapped by your KMS depending on config
(06:05) Priya Singh: can you speak to data residency? we have EU-only requirement for some cases
(06:12) Maya Chen: hosted regions are available in US and EU; you can pin data regions for model serving and storage. private gives you full control for on-prem. we also support contractual data processing addendums for residency needs
(06:30) Tom Hsu: about auditability — do you provide tamper-evident logs or integrated attestations for admin actions?
(06:40) Daniel Ortiz: we provide immutable append-only logs for control plane actions exposed through our audit API and you can ship them to your SIEM for long-term retention; for extra assurance you can enable signed log export where logs are SHA hashed before export
(06:58) Priya Singh: i heard mention of automatic fallbacks — if dedicated capacity is constrained how does the failover to hosted affect data exposure?
(07:10) Daniel Ortiz: good question — failover policies are configurable. by default we avoid sending traffic to hosted if request contains regulated flags; you can create policy rules that only allow fallback to model variants that don't touch sensitive payloads, or disable fallback entirely for certain routes
(07:35) Ethan Cole: network-level: do you support private endpoints and deny public internet access for nodes?
(07:45) Daniel Ortiz: in private and dedicated we support private endpoints, no public IPs on nodes, and optional NAT egress for controlled outbound. hosted does expose endpoints but you can lock by IP allowlist or private link
(08:05) Priya Singh: ok can we talk compliance for sub-processors? we need list of infra partners and cloud providers
(08:14) Maya Chen: yes we'll share our sub-processor list; it's in the security pack we send. we work with major cloud providers but can exclude partners for private/on-prem customers
(08:30) Priya Singh: about logging of model inputs — there are cases where our prompts contain PHI; we cannot have PHI stored in third-party storage. how do we guarantee no data persists?
(08:42) Daniel Ortiz: two options: hosted customers can opt out of logging model inputs; we also offer ephemeral-only modes where KV cache is ephemeral and not persisted. private gives you full control so no third-party storage is used — processing occurs inside your network and logs stay on-prem unless you export them
(09:05) Lina Park: for the bench tests, we want synthetic but realistic payloads and a 99th pctl SLA check. what tooling do you provide?
(09:15) Daniel Ortiz: we have a benchmark harness and can run with your payloads; we'll also share cost modeling sheets that show tokens per call and expected monthly spend across deployment modes
(09:30) Ethan Cole: any gotchas around data deletion requests — a regulator might ask us to remove data right away
(09:38) Maya Chen: we support data deletion workflows; for hosted we can purge stored logs and redacted artifacts on request and provide deletion evidence. in private, it's up to you to run deletion — we can provide tooling and guidance
(09:55) Tom Hsu: on liability and incident response — do you provide incident notification SLAs?
(10:02) Maya Chen: yes enterprise SLAs include incident notify windows and we have runbooks and a security team escalation channel; more detail in the security pack
(10:18) Priya Singh: great — i'd like to understand the attestation around key usage and KMS logs. can we see examples of KMS audit trails?
(10:27) Daniel Ortiz: we'll provide sample KMS audit logs and the steps for cross-account access. note some fields will be redacted in the hosted examples
(10:38) Maya Chen: quick recap — action items are: maya to send SOC2/ISO and sub-processor list; daniel to draft VPC/KMS diagram and run bench plan; priya to send retention classification and any legal requirements for data residency. we'll aim for a follow-up in two weeks for the bench results
(10:58) Priya Singh: that sounds good, thanks. one more question — do you support role-specific API keys that are scoped to model access only? we want to avoid leakage between services
(11:08) Daniel Ortiz: yes service tokens can be scoped to models, routes, and even prompt templates. they integrate with RBAC so you can tie keys to teams and rotate them via the API
(11:26) Ethan Cole: ok thanks everyone, we'll review materials once we get them and coordinate the bench inputs
(11:34) Maya Chen: perfect i'll follow up with the links and attachments, thanks all
(11:40) meeting end
